lessons.title: Frequency Tables and Cumulative Frequency
lessons.content:
Raw data is easier to read in a frequency table. Tally each value, count the tallies and write the frequency. When the data is continuous or spread over a wide range, group it into class intervals of equal width, such as 10 — 19, 20 — 29, 30 — 39; the intervals must not overlap, and the midpoint of each interval (14.5, 24.5, 34.5) is used for calculation. Grouped data loses the individual values, so give the class interval as the measure of spread rather than pretending to know each value.

The cumulative frequency column is a running total of the frequencies: each entry is the number of items up to and including that value or interval. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary to draw an ogive (cumulative frequency curve). From the ogive you read the median at half the total frequency, the lower quartile at one quarter and the upper quartile at three quarters, then find the interquartile range as Q3 — Q1, which describes the middle half of the data.

Worked example. If 40 students are surveyed, the median is read from the curve at cumulative frequency 20, the lower quartile at 10 and the upper quartile at 30. If these give 52, 44 and 61 marks, then the interquartile range is 61 — 44 = 17 marks and the semi-interquartile range is 8.5. For grouped data the estimated mean is Σfx ÷ Σf using the class midpoints, and the modal class is the interval with the highest frequency. Always answer in the units of the data.

The range is the simplest measure of spread: range = highest value − lowest value. For the data 12, 15, 15, 18, 22, 31 the range is 31 − 12 = 19. The range uses only two of the values, so one very large or very small reading changes it completely, which is why a question that quotes a range usually also asks for the interquartile range.

Quartiles cut the ordered data into four equal parts. The lower quartile Q1 is the value one quarter of the way through the data, the median Q2 is the halfway value and the upper quartile Q3 is the value three quarters of the way through. The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1, and it describes the middle half of the data, so it ignores the extreme values that the range depends on.

Worked method — the data 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15 with n = 8. Step 1, the range: 15 − 3 = 12. Step 2, the median: with 8 values the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th, so (8 + 9) ÷ 2 = 8.5. Step 3, the lower quartile: one quarter of the way through 8 values is position 2, so Q1 = 5. Step 4, the upper quartile: three quarters of the way through is position 6, so Q3 = 11. Step 5, the interquartile range: 11 − 5 = 6, so the middle half of the data spans 6 marks while the full range spans 12.

Analysing a statistical diagram means reading a fact off it and then saying what the fact means. The questions are always the same four: what is the highest or lowest, how many are in a given band, what fraction or percentage is in a band, and how does this group compare with another. Each is answered from the diagram's own axes, and the units come from the axis labels.

From an ogive the readings are cumulative, so the frequency in a band is the difference between two cumulative readings: if the curve reads 20 at 30 marks and 34 at 40 marks, then 34 − 20 = 14 students scored between 30 and 40 marks. From a histogram the frequency is the area of the bar, which for equal class widths is just its height; from a frequency polygon the peak is the modal class; from a bar chart the tallest bar is the most common category.

Worked method — an ogive of 40 students' marks reads 10 at 44 marks, 20 at 52 marks and 30 at 61 marks. Step 1, the median: half of 40 is 20, so the median is the mark at cumulative frequency 20, which is 52 marks. Step 2, the quartiles: one quarter of 40 is 10 and three quarters is 30, so Q1 = 44 marks and Q3 = 61 marks. Step 3, the interquartile range: 61 − 44 = 17 marks. Step 4, the number of students between 44 and 61 marks: 30 − 10 = 20 students, which is the middle half of the class, and 20 ÷ 40 = 50%, exactly as the quartiles promise.

Two traps. A cumulative reading is a running total, never the frequency in that single band, so always subtract. And a percentage read from a diagram must be quoted with its total: 20 out of 40 is 50%, and 20 out of 30 would be 66.7%, so the total matters as much as the count.

lessons.title: Data Types and Sampling
lessons.content:
Statistics starts with the group you want to know about. The population is every member of the group — every student in a school, every household in a parish, every light bulb in a factory run. A sample is a part chosen to represent the whole, and the whole point of a sample is that measuring it is cheaper and faster than measuring the population while still telling you something true about it. Data Types and Sampling is the vocabulary for both halves: what the group is, how it is measured, and what kind of number the answer is.

A census asks every member of the population, so it has no sampling error, but it costs time and money and it is impossible for a population that is being made or used up as you measure it. A survey is questions asked of a sample, and its quality depends entirely on how the sample was chosen. A random sample gives every member an equal chance of being picked; a biased sample — the first thirty people through the gate, or a poll taken only in one shop — over-represents whatever it is easiest to reach. A sample must be large enough to be reliable and random enough to be representative, and a bigger sample always beats a bigger questionnaire.

Numbers come in two kinds. Discrete data can take only whole-number values, because the thing being counted cannot be split: the number of students in a class, the number of cars in a car park, the number of goals in a match. Continuous data can take any value in a range, because the thing being measured can always be measured more precisely: a height of 1.62 m, a mass of 4.75 kg, a time of 12.4 s. The test is whether a value between two others makes sense — 3.5 students does not, but 3.5 kg does.

There is a second pair of words worth keeping. A variable is the quantity being recorded (height, income, favourite subject) and an observation is one recorded value of it. Categorical data records a label rather than a number, such as eye colour or the parish a student lives in; numerical data records a number, and is then either discrete or continuous. Age is continuous in principle and discrete in practice, because a form asks for it in whole years.

Worked method — a school of 1,200 students wants the average journey time to school. Step 1, name the population: every one of the 1,200 students. Step 2, decide between a census and a sample: a census means asking all 1,200 and has no sampling error, but it takes a week; a sample of 120 students chosen at random takes an afternoon. Step 3, check the sample: 120 is one tenth of the population, chosen at random, so it can represent the whole. Step 4, name the data type: journey time is continuous data, because it can take any value in a range such as 12.5 minutes, so it is recorded to the nearest minute. Step 5, state the conclusion with its limitation: the sample mean estimates the population mean, and the estimate is more reliable for a larger random sample.

lessons.title: Statistical Diagrams
lessons.content:
A statistical diagram is a picture of a frequency table, and each picture answers a different question. Choosing the right one is half the marks: a bar chart compares separate categories, a pie chart shows the share of a total, a histogram shows how grouped continuous data is spread, and a frequency polygon and an ogive show a shape or a running total.

A bar chart draws bars with gaps between them, one bar per category, with the height of the bar equal to the frequency. The gaps are the point: they say the categories are separate and could be reordered, so a bar chart may be drawn with the bars in any order, and for honest comparison its axis should start at zero.

A pie chart is one circle cut into sectors, one per category, and each sector's share is the category's proportion of the total. The angle of a sector comes from the same proportion: the pie-chart angle is (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. A survey of 40 students in which 10 walk to school gives 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25 of the circle, so the sector angle is 0.25 × 360° = 90°. The proportions must add to 1 and the angles to 360°, which is the check that catches an arithmetic slip.

Grouped continuous data is drawn as a histogram: bars with no gaps, for grouped data whose classes touch at their boundaries, and the width of each bar is the width of its class. A histogram sits on the class boundaries rather than the midpoints, which is what separates it from a bar chart.

A frequency polygon is the class midpoints joined by straight lines, so it shows the shape of the distribution — where it peaks and how it tails off. An ogive is cumulative frequency plotted against the upper class boundary of each class, and it is the diagram the quartiles are read from.

Worked method — 60 students' marks are grouped into the classes 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 with frequencies 8, 22, 20, 10. Step 1, total the frequencies: 8 + 22 + 20 + 10 = 60. Step 2, the pie-chart angle for the first class: (8 ÷ 60) × 360° = 48°. Step 3, check the rest: (22 ÷ 60) × 360° = 132°, (20 ÷ 60) × 360° = 120° and (10 ÷ 60) × 360° = 60°, and 48 + 132 + 120 + 60 = 360°, so the angles are correct. Step 4, the same class as a percentage of the total: 8 ÷ 60 = 0.133 to 3 decimal places, so 13.3% of the students scored under 10.

Relative frequency is the general name for that share: relative frequency = frequency ÷ total frequency, and it is a proportion between 0 and 1 that becomes a percentage when multiplied by 100. The pie-chart angle is simply the relative frequency multiplied by 360°, so the two halves of this topic are one calculation seen twice. A relative frequency table is the honest way to compare two groups of different sizes, because the totals no longer matter.

Two traps. A pie chart of raw counts and a pie chart of relative frequencies look identical, because the angles are the same, so always label which one you drew. And a histogram's bars are not interchangeable with a bar chart's: a bar chart has gaps and a histogram does not, so drawing grouped continuous data with gaps is wrong.

lessons.title: Standard Deviation
lessons.content:
The mean, median and mode say where the middle of a data set is; they say nothing about how far the values are spread around it. Two classes can both average 60 marks while one is tightly bunched and the other runs from 20 to 100. Standard Deviation is the measure of spread that uses every value, so it is the one to quote when two data sets must be compared.

The calculation is a short list of steps and every step has a name. Start with the mean: add the values and divide by how many there are. Then, for each value, write its deviation, which is the value minus the mean. Some deviations are negative and some are positive, and they always add to zero, which is why they cannot be averaged directly. So square each one: the squared deviation is the deviation multiplied by itself, and squaring makes every one of them positive. The variance is the mean of the squared deviations — add the squared deviations and divide by how many there are. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, which brings the answer back to the units of the data.

Worked method — the data set 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Step 1, the mean: 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Step 2, the deviations: 4 − 8 = −4, 6 − 8 = −2, 8 − 8 = 0, 10 − 8 = 2 and 12 − 8 = 4, and they add to 0 as they must. Step 3, the squared deviations: 16, 4, 0, 4 and 16. Step 4, the variance: 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Step 5, the standard deviation: √8 = 2.83 to 2 decimal places, so the standard deviation is about 2.83.

Compare that with a second set, 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, which also has a mean of 8. Its squared deviations are 36, 9, 0, 9 and 36, so the variance is 90 ÷ 5 = 18 and the standard deviation is √18 = 4.24 to 2 decimal places. Both sets average 8, but the second has the larger standard deviation, so its values are more spread out — that comparison is exactly what standard deviation is for.

A small standard deviation means the values cluster around the mean and the mean is a reliable summary; a large standard deviation means they are scattered and the mean hides a lot. The range is the crudest measure of the same thing — highest value minus lowest value — and it uses only two values, so a single outlier can change it completely while leaving the standard deviation almost untouched.

Two traps. Divide by how many values there are, not by how many deviations you wrote down after dropping the zero, and square before you average, never after. And a standard deviation is never negative and carries the same units as the data, so a standard deviation of 2.83 marks is right and −2.83 marks is impossible.

lessons.title: Statistical Inference
lessons.content:
Statistical inference is the step that turns a sample back into a statement about the whole population. You measured 120 students; the school has 1,200; inference is the sentence that connects the two. Statistical Inference is the discipline of making that sentence honest: saying what the sample supports, what it does not, and how much trust the number deserves.

An inference is a conclusion about a population drawn from a sample. It is never a certainty: it is an estimate with a reason attached. 'About one student in ten walks to school' is an inference, because the 120 students who were asked stand in for the 1,200 who were not. The moment the sample is biased, the inference is worthless however large it is — a poll taken only at the school gate will find more walkers than the school actually has.

A prediction is a statement about a value not yet measured, and it is a special case of inference. If a random sample of 120 students averages 12.5 minutes of travel, the predicted mean for all 1,200 is 12.5 minutes, and the predicted number of students taking more than 20 minutes is the sample's proportion multiplied by 1,200. Scale the sample result up by the ratio of the two sizes and you have the prediction.

A comparison puts two samples placed side by side and asks whether the difference is real or is just sampling variation. If one sample of 50 averages 61 marks and another sample of 50 averages 63 marks, a two-mark difference may be noise, and the honest answer is that the samples are too small to tell. The larger the samples and the larger the gap, the more confident the comparison.

A representative sample is one chosen so the sample mirrors the population: the same mix of ages, the same proportion of boys and girls, the same spread of parishes. A larger sample gives a more reliable estimate, because the effect of one unusual value shrinks as the sample grows, but size cannot repair a biased method. Reliability is how much a repeated sample would agree with the first: take another random 120 students and the mean should land close to the first, and the closer it lands, the more reliable the estimate.

Worked method — a random sample of 120 of the school's 1,200 students is asked their travel time and the sample mean is 12.5 minutes, with 30 of the 120 taking more than 20 minutes. Step 1, state the inference: the population mean travel time is about 12.5 minutes, estimated from a random sample of one tenth of the school. Step 2, the proportion in the sample: 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25, so a quarter of the sample takes more than 20 minutes. Step 3, predict for the population: 0.25 × 1,200 = 300 students. Step 4, state the limitation: the prediction is only as good as the sample, so it is reliable because the sample was random and large, and it would be wrong to quote 300 as an exact count.

Two traps. Never quote a sample result as if it were a census — the words 'about' and 'estimated from a sample' belong in the answer. And never compare two groups of very different sizes by their totals; compare their means, their proportions or their relative frequencies, because a bigger group has a bigger total for no better reason than its size.

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area
lessons.content:
Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a 2D shape. For a rectangle, it is 2(length + width); for a circle, the perimeter is called the circumference and is calculated using the formula C = 2πr or C = πd. Finding the perimeter is essentially like measuring the length of a fence needed to enclose a yard.

Area is the amount of space inside the boundaries of a flat 2D object, measured in square units (like cm² or m²). The area of a rectangle is length × width, while the area of a triangle is 1/2 × base × height. For a circle, the area is πr². More complex shapes can often be broken down into these basic forms to find the total area.

CSEC problems frequently involve compound shapes, such as a rectangle with a semi-circle on top. To solve these, calculate the area of each part separately and then add them together. Accuracy with units and formulas is key. Remember: perimeter is a length (1D), while area is a surface (2D).

An arc is a part of a circle’s circumference, and a sector is the region enclosed by two radii and an arc. The arc is the same fraction of the whole circle as the angle at the centre is of 360°, so arc length = θ/360 × 2πr. The perimeter of a sector is that arc plus the two radii: sector perimeter = θ/360 × 2πr + 2r.

Worked method — arc length and sector perimeter for a sector with radius r = 9 cm and angle θ = 80°, using π ≈ 3.142. Step 1, the fraction of the circle: θ/360 = 80/360 = 2/9. Step 2, the whole circumference: 2πr = 2 × 3.142 × 9 = 56.56 cm. Step 3, the arc: 2/9 × 56.56 = 12.57 cm. Step 4, the perimeter: add the two radii, 12.57 + 9 + 9 = 30.57 cm, so the sector perimeter is about 30.6 cm.

Parallelograms and trapeziums are handled by cutting them into rectangles and triangles. The area of a parallelogram = base × perpendicular height, where the height is measured perpendicular to the base and not along the slant side. The area of a trapezium = 1/2 × (a + b) × h, where a and b are the two parallel sides and h is the perpendicular distance between them.

Worked method — area of a trapezium with parallel sides a = 6 cm and b = 10 cm and height h = 4 cm. Add the parallel sides: a + b = 6 + 10 = 16 cm. Halve that sum: 1/2 × 16 = 8 cm. Multiply by the height: 8 × 4 = 32 cm², so the area of the trapezium is 32 cm².

To estimate the area of an irregular shape, split it into rectangles and triangles, or draw it on squared paper and count the squares it covers. For a circle, estimate with area = πr² and π ≈ 3.142 before rounding. An estimate is worth writing down even when an exact formula exists, because it shows whether the exact answer is the right size.

The area of a sector is the same fraction of the whole circle as the arc: sector area = θ/360 × πr². A segment is the region between a chord and its arc, and its area is the sector minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord: segment area = θ/360 × πr² − 1/2 × r² × sin θ. A triangle’s area is 1/2 × base × perpendicular height, or 1/2 × a × b × sin C when two sides and the angle between them are known.

Worked method — area of a segment with radius r = 6 cm and angle θ = 60°. Step 1, the sector: θ/360 × πr² = 60/360 × 3.142 × 36 = 18.85 cm². Step 2, the triangle: 1/2 × r² × sin θ = 1/2 × 36 × 0.8660 = 15.59 cm². Step 3, subtract: 18.85 − 15.59 = 3.26 cm², so the segment area is about 3.26 cm².

Keep the units straight to the end: an arc, a perimeter and a radius are lengths in cm, while a sector, a segment, a trapezium and a parallelogram are areas in cm².

Worked method — a rectangle with length l = 3 cm and width w = 4 cm. Area: A = l × w = 3 × 4 = 12 cm². Perimeter: P = 2(l + w) = 2(3 + 4) = 14 cm. A circle with radius r = 3 cm, using π ≈ 3.142: area A = πr² = 3.142 × 9 = 28.28 cm² and circumference C = 2πr = 2 × 3.142 × 3 = 18.85 cm. These are the two shapes the Area Builder resizes: drag the Length and Width sliders, or the Radius slider, and the Area and Perimeter readouts change with them — the Circumference is the perimeter of a circle.

lessons.title: Volume and Capacity
lessons.content:
Volume is the amount of 3D space an object occupies, measured in cubic units (like cm³ or m³). For prisms (shapes with a uniform cross-section), the volume is calculated by multiplying the area of the base by the height: V = A_base × h. This applies to cubes, rectangular prisms, and cylinders.

The volume of a cylinder is therefore πr²h, since its base is a circle. Capacity refers to the amount of liquid a container can hold. While volume is the physical space occupied by the object, capacity is often expressed in litres (L) or millilitres (mL). A key conversion to remember for CSEC is that 1000 cm³ = 1 litre.

In exams, you might be asked to find the volume of a water tank or determine how many small boxes can fit into a larger container. Some problems also involve 'displacement' — when an object is submerged in water, the volume of water it displaces is equal to its own volume. Always double-check your formula and ensure your units are consistent.

Worked method — a rectangular prism with length 4 cm, width 3 cm and height 5 cm. Base area: A_base = length × width = 4 × 3 = 12 cm². Volume: V = A_base × h = 12 × 5 = 60 cm³. Capacity: 1 L = 1000 cm³, so 60 ÷ 1000 = 0.06 L. A cylinder with radius 3 cm filled to a height of 10 cm, using π ≈ 3.142: V = πr²h = 3.142 × 9 × 10 = 282.78 cm³, and 282.78 ÷ 1000 = 0.283 L (3 s.f.). The Volume Lab fills a rectangular prism and a cylinder to any height you choose and shows the Base area, the Volume in cm³ and the Capacity in litres as the water rises.

lessons.title: SI Units, Conversion and Rates
lessons.content:
The International System (SI) uses base units: the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time and the ampere (A) for current. Prefixes scale these units — kilo means 1000, centi means 1/100, milli means 1/1000 and micro means 1/1,000,000 — so 1 km = 1000 m, 1 cm = 0.01 m and 1 mg = 0.001 g. Because area is measured in square units, 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10,000 cm²; because volume is measured in cubic units, 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³. Capacity and volume are linked: 1 cm³ = 1 mL and 1 m³ = 1000 L.

A rate compares two quantities with different units. Speed is the commonest: speed = distance ÷ time, distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed. To change km/h into m/s, multiply by 1000/3600 = 5/18; to change m/s into km/h, multiply by 18/5. A car travelling at 72 km/h covers 72 × 5/18 = 20 m each second. Density (mass ÷ volume), flow rate (litres per minute) and fuel consumption (km per litre) are handled the same way, and the unit of the answer comes from the units you divided.

Conversion questions ask you to change one unit to another by multiplying or dividing by a power of ten, and it is worth checking that the answer is sensible: a distance in metres should be much larger than in kilometres. Time needs care because it is not decimal — 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes, and 2 hours 45 minutes is 2.75 hours, not 2.45 hours. In measurement problems, copy the given values with their units, convert to a single system, then calculate, and state the unit with the final answer.

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind, written with a colon as 45:60 or as the fraction 45/60. Simplifying a ratio means dividing every part by the highest common factor: 45 and 60 share 15, so 45:60 = 3:4. A ratio has no units, because the two quantities cancel, which is why 45 minutes to 60 minutes and 45 km to 60 km simplify the same way.

A rate is a ratio whose two quantities have different units, so a rate keeps its units: 240 km in 3 hours is the rate 80 km/h, and $12 for 4 pens is the rate $3 per pen. A rate is read with the word per, and its unit is the unit of the first quantity divided by the unit of the second.

Two quantities are in direct proportion when one is a constant multiple of the other, written y = kx: doubling x doubles y. Find k from the pair you are given, then use it. If 5 m of cloth costs $120 then k = 120 ÷ 5 = 24 dollars per metre, so 8 m costs 8 × 24 = $192, and k is the unit rate.

Two quantities are in inverse proportion when their product stays the same, written y = k/x: doubling x halves y. If 4 workers take 12 days, the work is 4 × 12 = 48 worker-days, so k = 48 and 6 workers take 48 ÷ 6 = 8 days. The direction of the change is the test: if both quantities rise together the proportion is direct, and if one rises while the other falls it is inverse.

Worked method — an applied measurement problem. A tank is 1.2 m long, 0.8 m wide and 0.5 m deep and is filled at 15 litres per minute. Step 1, the volume: 1.2 × 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.48 m³. Step 2, convert to the unit the rate uses: 1 m³ = 1000 L, so 0.48 m³ = 480 L. Step 3, the time: 480 ÷ 15 = 32 minutes. Check: 32 × 15 = 480 L, so the tank takes 32 minutes to fill.

Every applied measurement question has that same three-step shape: find the measurement, convert it to the unit the rate uses, then divide or multiply by the rate — and state the unit with the answer.

lessons.title: Surface Area of Solids
lessons.content:
Surface area is the total area of every face of a solid, measured in square units such as cm² or m². Volume says how much space is inside a solid; surface area says how much material it takes to cover the outside. Surface Area of Solids is the method for finding that total from the dimensions you are given, one face at a time.

A net is the solid opened out and laid flat, so a net turns one 3D problem into a set of 2D ones. The net of a cube is six equal squares. The net of a cuboid is six rectangles in three matching pairs: top and bottom, front and back, and the two ends. The net of a triangular prism is two triangles and three rectangles. No picture is needed to use a net — name each face in words, write down its dimensions, and the sum of the faces is the surface area.

For a cube with side s, all six faces are squares of area s², so surface area = 6 × side²: a cube of side 4 cm has surface area 6 × 16 = 96 cm². For a cuboid with length l, width w and height h, the three different faces are lw, lh and wh and each appears twice, so surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh).

A prism is handled by its two ends and its sides: surface area = 2 × area of the base + perimeter of the base × length of the prism. A cylinder is the case where the base is a circle, so its two ends are circles of area πr² and its curved side opens out into a rectangle of width 2πr and height h. That gives the cylinder formula: surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh.

Read the question for the face that is missing. An open-top tank has no lid, so subtract the top face from the total. A pipe open at both ends has only its curved surface, 2πrh. Every length must be in the same unit before you square or multiply it, and the answer is always in square units, never in cubic units.

Worked method — surface area of a cuboid 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm. Label the faces: two faces of 8 × 5 = 40 cm², two faces of 8 × 3 = 24 cm² and two faces of 5 × 3 = 15 cm². Add them: 2 × 40 + 2 × 24 + 2 × 15 = 80 + 48 + 30 = 158 cm². Check with the formula: 2(lw + lh + wh) = 2(40 + 24 + 15) = 2 × 79 = 158 cm², so the surface area is 158 cm².

Worked method — surface area of a cylinder with radius r = 7 cm and height h = 10 cm, using π ≈ 3.142. The two ends: 2πr² = 2 × 3.142 × 49 = 307.9 cm². The curved surface: 2πrh = 2 × 3.142 × 7 × 10 = 439.9 cm². Add them: 307.9 + 439.9 = 747.8 cm², so the surface area is about 748 cm².
objectives: Name each face of a solid and add the face areas to find its surface area (Surface Area of Solids)
Unfold a cube, cuboid or prism into a net described face by face (Surface Area of Solids)
Use 6 × side² for a cube and 2(lw + lh + wh) for a cuboid (Surface Area of Solids)
Use 2πr² + 2πrh for the ends and curved surface of a cylinder (Surface Area of Solids)
Adjust the total for an open top or an open pipe (Surface Area of Solids)
concepts: Surface area is the total area of every face, measured in square units.
A net is the solid opened out flat, so the area of the net is the surface area.
Cube: surface area = 6 × side².
Cuboid: surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh).
Cylinder: surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh.
An open top or an open pipe leaves one or both faces out of the total.

lessons.title: Measurement Error
lessons.content:
No measurement is exact: a ruler reads to the nearest millimetre, a kitchen scale to the nearest 0.1 kg, and the true value stays hidden between the marks. Measurement Error is how a measurement is described once you say how far it could be from the truth — as an absolute error, a relative error or a percentage error.

Absolute error is the size of the difference between the measured value and the true value, in the units of the measurement: absolute error = measured value − true value. The sign is ignored, because a measurement can be too high or too low. If a rod’s true length is 24.8 cm and it is measured as 25 cm, the absolute error is 25 − 24.8 = 0.2 cm.

Relative error compares that difference with the true value, so it has no units: relative error = absolute error ÷ true value. For the rod, 0.2 ÷ 24.8 = 0.0081 to 3 significant figures. Percentage error puts the same comparison in hundredths: percentage error = relative error × 100, so 0.0081 × 100 = 0.81% to 2 decimal places.

Bounds come from the rounding. A value written to d decimal places could be anything from x − 0.5 × 10⁻ᵈ up to x + 0.5 × 10⁻ᵈ, because the true value was rounded to the nearest 10⁻ᵈ, so the greatest possible error is 0.5 × 10⁻ᵈ. A mass recorded as 4.6 kg to 1 d.p. has bounds 4.55 kg to 4.65 kg, because its greatest possible error is 0.5 × 10⁻¹ = 0.05 kg. A length recorded as 25 cm to the nearest cm has bounds 24.5 cm to 25.5 cm, because 0.5 × 10⁰ = 0.5 cm.

Worked method — a rod measures 25 cm to the nearest cm and its true length is 24.8 cm. Step 1, the bounds: the greatest possible error is 0.5 × 10⁰ = 0.5 cm, so the true length lies between 24.5 cm and 25.5 cm. Step 2, the absolute error: 25 − 24.8 = 0.2 cm. Step 3, the relative error: 0.2 ÷ 24.8 = 0.0081 to 3 significant figures. Step 4, the percentage error: 0.0081 × 100 = 0.81%, so the measurement is about 0.81% too high.

Two traps. The denominator of a relative error is the true value, never the measured value, and a percentage error carries no units. When two measured quantities are combined, their absolute errors add for a sum or a difference, and their percentage errors add for a product or a quotient.
objectives: Calculate the absolute error of a measurement (Measurement Error)
Calculate the relative error and the percentage error (Measurement Error)
Find the lower and upper bounds of a value written to d decimal places (Measurement Error)
State the greatest possible error of a rounded measurement (Measurement Error)
concepts: Absolute error = measured value − true value, in the units of the measurement.
Relative error = absolute error ÷ true value, and it has no units.
Percentage error = relative error × 100.
A value rounded to d decimal places lies between x − 0.5 × 10⁻ᵈ and x + 0.5 × 10⁻ᵈ.
The greatest possible error of a rounded value is 0.5 × 10⁻ᵈ.

lessons.title: Scale and Scale Drawings
lessons.content:
A scale drawing is a copy of a real object with every length shrunk by the same factor, so the drawing keeps the shape and changes only the size. Scale and Scale Drawings is about the ratio between the drawing and the real thing, and about moving a length from one to the other without losing the units.

A scale is written as a ratio, drawing : real, and 1:50 is read aloud as one to fifty. A scale of 1:50 means 1 cm on the drawing is 50 cm real, which is 0.5 m. Real length = drawing length × scale factor, and drawing length = real length ÷ scale factor, so at 1:50 the scale factor is 50 and the units must match before you multiply.

Worked method — a wall drawn 7 cm at 1:50. Step 1, write the scale as a ratio: drawing : real = 1 : 50. Step 2, multiply the drawing length by the scale factor: 7 × 50 = 350 cm. Step 3, convert to a sensible unit: 350 cm = 3.5 m, so the real wall is 3.5 m long. Going the other way, a 4 m wall is 400 cm real, and 400 ÷ 50 = 8 cm on the drawing.

Maps use the same idea with larger numbers. A map scale of 1:25,000 means 1 cm on the map is 250 m, because 25,000 cm = 250 m = 0.25 km. A distance of 6 cm on that map is 6 × 25,000 = 150,000 cm = 1,500 m = 1.5 km.

Areas need the square of the scale factor, because a length factor is applied twice. At 1:50 the length factor is 50 and the area scale factor is 50² = 2500. A room 4 m by 3 m drawn at 1:50 measures 8 cm by 6 cm, an area of 48 cm² on the drawing, so the real area is 48 × 2500 = 120,000 cm² = 12 m², which agrees with 4 m × 3 m = 12 m².

Two traps. A scale of 1:50 does not mean the drawing is one fiftieth of a metre; it means every length is one fiftieth of the real length, in whatever unit you use. And a scale never changes an angle: the angles on a scale drawing are the real angles, which is why a drawing to scale can be used to measure an angle that cannot be measured on the object itself.
objectives: Read a scale written as a ratio such as 1:50 (Scale and Scale Drawings)
Convert a drawing length to a real length and back again (Scale and Scale Drawings)
Use a map scale such as 1:25,000 to find a real distance (Scale and Scale Drawings)
Use the area scale factor to find a real area from a scale drawing (Scale and Scale Drawings)
concepts: A scale is a ratio, drawing : real, written 1:50 and read as one to fifty.
1:50 means 1 cm on the drawing is 50 cm real.
Real length = drawing length × scale factor.
Drawing length = real length ÷ scale factor.
Areas scale by the square of the length factor: 50² = 2500 at 1:50.
